title: The Steersman and the Noise: Norbert Wiener, Cybernetics, and the Macy Conferences
search_title: Norbert Wiener, Cybernetics, and the Macy Conferences: History and Legacy
description: An essay on how a child prodigy turned wartime mathematician invented cybernetics, the science of feedback and control, and how the Macy conferences of 1946 to 1953 tried and failed to turn it into a unified science of mind, machine, and society. It argues that the conferences' greatest achievement was not synthesis but cross-contamination: a generation of scientists who left with new questions.
standfirst: In 1946, the most brilliant collection of minds in postwar America gathered in a New York hotel room to build a science that might explain everything. They met nine more times, and the science was never quite built.
body:
## A Yellow Cover In the late winter of 1942, an unusual document arrived at the offices of the National Defense Research Committee in Washington. It was bound in yellow, ran to several hundred pages, and was stamped classified. The mathematics inside was of a kind that only a handful of people in the country could follow, and those who tried and failed to follow it gave the report its nickname: the Yellow Peril.1 Its author was Norbert Wiener, a forty-seven-year-old professor of mathematics at MIT, and its subject was the problem of shooting down an aircraft. The problem sounds mechanical, but Wiener had made it philosophical. An anti-aircraft gun cannot aim at where a plane is; by the time the shell arrives, the plane has moved. The gun must aim at where the plane will be. And the plane is flown by a pilot who is trying, with every nerve in his body, not to be where the shell will be. So the gun's gunner is not targeting a machine but a mind, and the question of how to hit that mind is a question about the relationship between past behaviour and future intent.2 Working with his MIT engineer Julian Bigelow, Wiener developed a statistical predictor that treated the pilot's flight path as a time series to be analysed and extrapolated. The theory he built was general enough to describe any process of communication corrupted by noise, any effort to extract signal from interference. It would, in time, become known as the Wiener filter, and it laid part of the groundwork for what we now call information theory.3 But in 1942, the army found it impractical and chose a less sophisticated system instead. The Yellow Peril was classified, filed, and not published openly until 1949. Wiener, characteristically, took this as an opportunity to think. What he and Bigelow had noticed, working on the predictor, was something that seemed to go beyond engineering. The gunner trying to track a plane and the pilot trying to evade the shell were each using feedback: information about the gap between where they were and where they wanted to be, used to close that gap. This was exactly how the thermostat and the steam governor worked, the same loop by which the body maintains its temperature and its balance. Wiener's engineer had an instinct, and Wiener's mathematician had the mathematics to formalise it: feedback was not a trick of machinery but a principle of purposeful behaviour in general, in animals and machines alike.4 ## Purpose Without a Soul In January 1943, Wiener published, with Bigelow and his old friend the Mexican physiologist Arturo Rosenblueth, a short paper called "Behavior, Purpose and Teleology" in the journal *Philosophy of Science*.5 It is one of the stranger and more consequential papers in the history of science, and it is worth pausing on what it did. For centuries, the idea of *purpose* had been a problem for science. Machines did not have purposes; they had causes. Rocks fell because of gravity, not because they wanted to reach the ground. Only living things, and especially minds, seemed to pursue goals, to reach toward a future state. Aristotle had called this teleology, and while Aristotle was no longer fashionable, the puzzle he identified had not gone away. How do you explain behaviour that is directed toward a future state without invoking something non-mechanical, something like a soul or a will? Wiener, Rosenblueth, and Bigelow proposed an answer. Any system whose current state is modified by the gap between its current state and its goal is behaving purposefully, in a scientifically precise sense, without any metaphysics required. A missile that corrects its trajectory based on radar returns is behaving purposefully. So is a cat reaching for a mouse. The difference between them is of degree, not of kind. As the authors put it, they were defining teleological behaviour as "purposive" but controlled by feedback, and in doing so they believed they were rescuing the concept of purpose from vitalism on one side and dismissal on the other.6 This was an extraordinary move. It unified the vocabulary of engineering with the vocabulary of biology, and suggested that the same mathematics could describe both. It was not, to be sure, the first time anyone had noticed that machines could mimic purposive behaviour. The eighteenth century was full of clever automata. But Wiener's group had something the automaton-builders lacked: a rigorous way to talk about information, error, and correction as a single loop. That same year, the neurophysiologist Warren McCulloch and the runaway teenage logician Walter Pitts published a paper of matching ambition: "A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity." In it they proposed that neurons could be modelled as logical switches, and that networks of such switches could compute any logical function. They were proposing, in essence, that the brain was a kind of computer.7 McCulloch and Pitts were not at that point acquainted with Wiener. But by 1943, three of the founding ideas of artificial intelligence had appeared in print: feedback-governed purposive behaviour, formal models of neural computation, and the statistical theory of communication that would become information theory. The remarkable thing is that all three emerged in the same year, in the same intellectual world around MIT, without any of the authors quite knowing what the others were doing. ## The Word Wiener had by now a name in mind for the science he was building. He took it from the Greek *kybernetes*, meaning the steersman of a ship, the person who holds the tiller. James Clerk Maxwell had used the Latin derivative *governor* in an 1868 paper on feedback in steam engines, the paper that Wiener explicitly cited as a predecessor. The French physicist André-Marie Ampère had proposed *cybernétique* as a name for the science of government in the early nineteenth century, but the word had been forgotten. Wiener revived it and gave it a new meaning: the science of control and communication in the animal and the machine.8 In 1948, he published a book with that subtitle. *Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine* was first issued in Paris by Hermann et Cie, and then in a matching American edition by John Wiley in New York. The first edition was set in France, which may explain why Wiener did not read the proofs carefully: the book was full of typographical errors, which persisted through multiple printings until a corrected second edition appeared in 1961.9 It was a peculiar object: dense with equations in some chapters, wide-ranging and speculative in others, veering from Newtonian time to information theory to neurophysiology to philosophy. It was not written for a popular audience. The first American edition nevertheless went through at least five printings in 1948 alone, and was reviewed in *Time Magazine* on December 27 of that year under the headline "In Man's Image."10 The public fascination was real and a little anxious. Wiener was proposing something that disturbed the settled boundary between the mechanical and the living. If feedback explained purposive behaviour, and if the brain was a logical machine, then the difference between a calculating machine and a human being was perhaps a matter of complexity rather than of essence. That was not a comfortable thought in 1948, though Wiener himself seems to have found it clarifying rather than threatening. He was, by most accounts, a complicated and not entirely comfortable man, and it suited him to find that the most intimate processes of life were subject to mathematical description. ## A Hotel Room in New York Before the book appeared, there had already been meetings. The Josiah Macy, Jr. Foundation was a New York philanthropy with an unusual idea about scientific progress. Conventional conferences brought specialists together to hear finished work from other specialists. The Macy format was different: preliminary, unpublished research was presented to an audience drawn from many different fields, and discussion was deliberately prolonged and unruly. The aim was not to advance a single discipline but to find the vocabulary that might connect several of them.11 The first of the cybernetics-related Macy conferences met in New York on 8 and 9 March 1946, under the title "Feedback Mechanisms and Circular Causal Systems in Biological and Social Systems." The organiser on behalf of the Foundation was Frank Fremont-Smith, who opened the meeting with a remark that was equal parts aspiration and experiment: each group, he told the participants, was itself an experiment, and if they found it interesting enough they would meet again.12 They found it interesting enough. The core group that gathered in March 1946 included Wiener; McCulloch, who would chair all ten conferences; Bigelow; Rosenblueth; John von Neumann; the anthropologists Gregory Bateson and Margaret Mead; the neurophysiologist Ralph Gerard; the ecologist G. Evelyn Hutchinson; the psychiatrist Lawrence Kubie; the psychologist Molly Harrower; the sociologist Paul Lazarsfeld; and Walter Pitts.12 The title of the conference changed at nearly every meeting as the participants tried and failed to agree on what, exactly, they were studying. By the fourth conference, in October 1947, it had become "Circular Causal and Feedback Mechanisms in Biological and Social Systems." Not until the sixth conference, in March 1949, did it acquire the name that would stick. This came about because Heinz von Foerster, a young Austrian biophysicist attending his first Macy meeting, suggested adopting Wiener's recently coined term "cybernetics" as the conference title on the grounds that it was mercifully shorter. The proposal was enthusiastically approved, and Wiener, according to von Foerster's later recollections, was so moved that he left the room to hide his tears.13 The conferences were not titled or characterised as cybernetics conferences until six of the ten had already taken place. The name arrived more than halfway through. ## What They Talked About The first five conferences were never formally transcribed with published proceedings, which means they are known only through retrospective summaries and the notes of participants. This is a significant lacuna: by most accounts the early conferences were the most energetic, before the novelty wore thin and the participants began to prioritise other demands on their time. The last five conferences were published, and they were edited by von Foerster, with Mead and Hans-Lukas Teuber as assistant editors.14 What was actually discussed across the decade? The scholar Jean-Pierre Dupuy attempted a taxonomy, and his categories are illuminating. The largest single topic, accounting for seventeen discussion units in his count, was the applicability of a logic-machine model to both brain and computer: this was essentially McCulloch's question, prosecuted with remarkable persistence by McCulloch and Pitts against the scepticism of the psychologists and psychiatrists in the room. The second largest was human and social communication. The third was analogies between organisms and machines, which Dupuy associates with Wiener's particular interests. Next came neuroses and the pathology of mental life, driven largely by the persistent presentations of the psychoanalyst Lawrence Kubie, who refused to be shouted down by the engineers. And then, strikingly, only five discussion units were given to what Dupuy calls "cybernetic machines", the robots and automata that in the popular imagination had come to define the whole enterprise.15 This last figure is a useful corrective. The newspapers in 1948 and 1949 were writing about robots and thinking machines as the product of this remarkable group, but the group itself was spending most of its time arguing about neurons, perception, and psychoanalysis. The arguments were genuine and sometimes fierce. The divide that runs through the entire conference series is between what participants called the analogue and the digital: between those, like McCulloch and Pitts, who wanted to model mind as a network of discrete logical switches, and those, like Gerard, who kept pointing out that the brain is a wet, continuous, biochemical organ that does not look much like a logic circuit. At the first conference, Gerard had commented that the brain's operations were more analogue than digital. By the seventh conference, in March 1950, he was making essentially the same point again, to the visible frustration of the more mathematically inclined participants. The argument was not resolved.16 The psychoanalysts presented a different kind of difficulty. Kubie's presentations on neurosis and compulsive behaviour were repeatedly met with criticism from Pitts, who could find no coherent theory in psychoanalysis, and from Bateson, who could find no objectivity. Kubie kept coming back. This persistence was itself a kind of argument: a reminder that the science of mind could not be reduced to circuit diagrams without losing something important, even if no one in the room could quite specify what that something was. Economists and political scientists never appeared at any of the ten conferences, though Wiener and von Neumann had, at the first meeting, expressed confidence their theories would illuminate both fields. F. S. C. Northrop, the sole philosopher in the core group, gave a presentation at the first conference on ethics and philosophy of science, found little response, and thereafter contributed little. The interdisciplinary ambition was real, but the disciplines that showed up were not quite the ones that had been hoped for.17 Claude Shannon appeared as a guest at three of the last four conferences, beginning with the seventh. His information theory, published in 1948 in the same extraordinary year as *Cybernetics*, gave the engineers in the room a precise language for signals, noise, and what a channel can carry. Shannon's presence pushed the later conferences somewhat toward the communication-engineering end of the spectrum, and somewhat away from the biological and psychoanalytic end. At the seventh conference he presented a formal analysis of statistical redundancy in printed English, tilting the discussion firmly away from the social scientists who had been energised by the previous presentation on speech intelligibility.18 Von Neumann is a more complicated case. He was a core group member from the beginning, and his authority in mathematics and computing was unrivalled. But he operated, as one commentator on the conference record notes, more like an outsider than an insider, pursuing his own agenda, attending irregularly, and by the eighth conference had effectively dropped out. He nonetheless cast a long shadow: at the sixth conference, a message from him (he was not present) proposing that the brain's complexity could not be accounted for by the number of its neurons alone set off a debate that was resolved only when Pitts identified an error in von Neumann's calculation.19 The anecdote is representative. Von Neumann did not need to be in the room to dominate it. Wiener himself dropped out after the seventh conference. He did not attend the eighth, in March 1951, or any subsequent meeting. The reasons, like so much in Wiener's life, are entangled with his marriage. ## The Break After the war, Wiener had helped MIT to recruit a cognitive science research group, bringing McCulloch and Pitts from Illinois to work alongside him in Cambridge. The collaboration was productive and apparently warm. Then, in 1951, Wiener severed all contact with McCulloch, Pitts, and everyone associated with them, without explanation. He sent a telegram to the president of MIT dissociating himself from any collaboration with the McCulloch group, and he never spoke to Pitts again.20 The biographers Flo Conway and Jim Siegelman, in their 2005 biography *Dark Hero of the Information Age*, argue that the break was engineered by Wiener's wife Margaret, who bore an intense hostility toward McCulloch and his bohemian circle. According to their account, she told Wiener a damaging and apparently false story about members of the group and their daughter. Wiener chose to believe it.21 McCulloch never understood why the friendship ended. Walter Pitts, who had come to regard Wiener as a father figure, was devastated. He burned his unpublished manuscripts, withdrew from academic life, and struggled with alcoholism until his death in 1969.22 The personal wreckage was real. And the break had intellectual consequences: it divided the two most important centres of cybernetic thinking in America just as the field was finding its identity, and it contributed to the fragmentation that would leave cybernetics without the institutional home it needed to survive as a discipline. The final Macy conference, in April 1953, was held at Princeton rather than New York, ostensibly for the convenience of von Neumann, who had for practical purposes dropped out three conferences earlier. The discussion was animated but, in Teuber's judgement, lacking in content. When McCulloch was asked to write a final summary of the consensus achieved over ten years, he produced a sentence in effect, that the participants had learned to know one another a little better and to argue in their shirtsleeves. The proceedings of the final conference were published only after Teuber threatened to resign if the discussion transcripts were included; in the end, only the papers appeared.23 ## The Rebel Scientist Meanwhile, Wiener had been doing something the other participants had not: speaking in public about what his science implied. The atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945 had shocked many scientists into moral reflection. For Wiener the shock was both ethical and personal. He had, throughout the war, worked on the anti-aircraft predictor in the belief that he was contributing to legitimate defence. The bombing of Japanese cities was not what he had signed up for. In January 1947, he published a short letter in *The Atlantic Monthly* under the title "A Scientist Rebels." In it he announced that he would no longer allow any of his work to be used by what he called "irresponsible militarists" to build weapons, and he called on other scientists to do the same.24 The letter had been triggered by a request from a researcher at an aircraft corporation for access to Wiener's wartime work on guided missiles. He refused, made the refusal public, and from that point refused all government funding and military contracts for the rest of his life.25 This position cost him. It put him at odds with the postwar funding system that was rebuilding American science around military contracts, and it meant that cybernetics, unlike many rival disciplines, could not draw on Pentagon money. It was one of the more principled and expensive decisions in the history of twentieth-century science. In 1950 he published *The Human Use of Human Beings: Cybernetics and Society*, a popular account of cybernetics and its social implications aimed at non-specialists. The book is now remembered largely for its warnings about automation, which were specific and grim. Wiener argued that machines capable of feedback and learning would render large categories of human labour redundant, and that this displacement would be socially catastrophic. The automatic machine was, he wrote, "the precise equivalent of slave labor," and any labour that competed with it would have to accept the economic conditions of slave labor. The resulting unemployment would, in his view, make "the depression of the thirties seem a pleasant joke."26 This was not a popular thing to say in 1950, in a country enjoying a postwar boom. It was dismissed at the time as alarmism. The question of whether it was correct is, on this essay's reading, still open. ## What Was Cybernetics? By the time the Macy conferences ended in 1953, cybernetics had produced several important things and failed to produce one important thing. What it produced: a common vocabulary for talking about feedback, information, and control across disciplines that had previously had no way to talk to each other. The concepts of input, output, and feedback, now so embedded in ordinary speech that their origin is invisible, spread from Wiener's work. The idea that the brain might usefully be compared to a computing machine, however inexact the comparison, opened research programmes in neurophysiology, psychology, and what would eventually become cognitive science. The McCulloch-Pitts neuron, the formal model proposed in 1943, became the ancestor of the perceptron and, at a long remove, of the neural networks that now dominate machine learning.27 The Macy conferences gave all of this a social location: a room where a biologist could argue with an engineer and an anthropologist could ask what a logical calculus had to do with how children learn. What cybernetics failed to produce was the unified science that Fremont-Smith had hoped for. As the American Society for Cybernetics has observed in its summary of the conference record, the Macy conferences were less an original birthplace than a breeding ground, and no one came out of them claiming to have been transformed into a "cybernetician."28 The disciplines pulled apart rather than together. By the mid-1950s, information theory was Shannon's field, computer science was becoming its own discipline, and cognitive science was developing its own journals and departments. Cybernetics, the name and the aspiration, was left without a home. In the Soviet Union, things went differently. Wiener's book was translated and read widely, and cybernetics became an officially sanctioned way of thinking about planning, management, and control, which created its own distortions, but also sustained the idea as a going concern for longer than it survived in the West. That Wiener's warnings about the dangers of information-processing systems were ideologically repurposed by the Soviet state to justify centralised control is one of the richer ironies in the history of ideas. Wiener died in Stockholm on 18 March 1964, aged sixty-nine, of a heart attack. He had received the National Medal of Science the year before, presented by President Johnson at a White House ceremony.29 His final book, *God and Golem, Inc.*, published in the year of his death, explored the theological implications of machines that learn and reproduce, machines that, in his view, would pose to their creators the same questions the golem posed to its maker. It won the National Book Award in 1965.30 ## The Absent-Minded Steersman Wiener is famous among mathematicians for absent-mindedness. The story most often told has him stopping a student on the MIT campus, asking which direction he had been heading, and explaining, on being told, that this meant he had already had his lunch. It is probably apocryphal, or at least improved in the retelling. What is not apocryphal is that he was, by any measure, extraordinary: a child who entered Tufts College at eleven and graduated at fourteen, who received his PhD from Harvard at nineteen, who studied with Bertrand Russell and G. H. Hardy at Cambridge and with David Hilbert at Göttingen, who joined MIT's mathematics department in 1919 and remained there until his death.31 The difficulty with Wiener is that his contributions go in several directions at once and do not resolve into a single line. He made foundational contributions to the theory of Brownian motion and stochastic processes. He developed the mathematics of harmonic analysis. He invented, independently of Shannon, the statistical treatment of communication as a branch of probability theory. He built, with Bigelow and Rosenblueth, the science of feedback-governed purposive behaviour that became cybernetics. And then he spent the last fifteen years of his life trying to persuade a largely indifferent public that this science had urgent social implications. He was right about the social implications. Whether the science itself, as he conceived it, was the right one remains less clear. The Macy conferences tried to generalise it across biology, psychology, anthropology, and sociology, and the generalisation did not hold together. The social scientists found the engineering metaphors too rigid; the engineers found the social scientists too vague. Gestalt psychology could not be expressed in circuit diagrams; psychoanalysis resisted every attempt to translate it into the vocabulary of error correction and feedback loops. The analogue-digital debate that ran across all ten conferences was never resolved because it was not, in the end, a technical disagreement: it was a disagreement about whether the mathematical formalisms of the engineers were the right tools for understanding mind. The debate is not over. Contemporary arguments about whether large neural networks are genuinely learning or merely pattern-matching, about whether feedback and reward are adequate concepts for describing intelligent behaviour, about whether the brain is better understood as a logic circuit or as a continuous dynamical system, these are recognisably the same arguments that Wiener, McCulloch, Pitts, Bateson, and Gerard were having in New York hotel rooms between 1946 and 1953. The names have changed and the mathematics has grown considerably more powerful, but the question underneath has not changed: what kind of thing is a mind, and can a machine have one? The comparison to current debates is this essay's, not the sources'. What Wiener added, and what his colleagues at the Macy conferences mostly did not, was insistence that the question was not purely technical. If a machine can approximate intelligent behaviour, then it can approximate it for good purposes and for bad ones. It can be used to liberate workers from drudgery, or to make them unnecessary. It can be a tool of communication or a tool of control. The steersman who holds the tiller steers somewhere: the question of where is not a mathematical question.
